metadata.purpose: Canonical terminology for the corpus, optimised for LLM ingestion. Authoritative source for naming choices when discussing the project.

terms.definition: Plural Hebrew noun, used throughout the Torah for the figures conventionally translated as God. The corpus reads the plural form at face value: a specific civilization of biological beings, not a deity. Always capitalize. Never translate as 'God' or 'gods' when speaking from inside the canon.

President of the Council of the Eternals on the Elohim civilization's home planet. Led the scientific team that established the Earth life-design project. Used for biblical YHWH references in canon voice; do not substitute 'God'.

The modern religious-philosophical movement founded by Claude Vorilhon (Raël) following his reported 1973 contact with the Elohim. Foundational canon (Tier 0) for the corpus. Note the diaeresis on the ë. Do not write 'Raelism' or 'Raelianism'.
One complete precessional cycle of Earth's axis — approximately 25,920 years. The corpus's largest temporal unit. The first Great Year (the creation project) is closing; the second is beginning.
One of the twelve approximately-2,160-year periods that subdivide the Great Year, each named for its zodiacal constellation. The corpus's organizing framework for long-form narrative.
The ~25,920-year wobble of Earth's axis that produces the slow westward drift of the vernal equinox through the constellations. Observed by Hipparchus (~150 BCE). The corpus's chronological backbone.
Deliberative body of approximately 700 members on the Elohim home world; the governance structure under which the Earth project is conducted.
The Hebrew term in Genesis 6 — 'the fallen ones'. Read in the corpus as the offspring of contact between Elohim officers and human women during the late pre-Flood period.
1969 study by Giorgio de Santillana and Hertha von Dechend on precessional encoding in ancient mythology. Foundational reference for the corpus's chronological method.

The broader academic and popular label for readings that take ancient testimony of celestial visitors as historical rather than mythological. The corpus engages this literature critically — distinct from popular ancient-astronaut media.
